lesson.title: When Old Memories Crowd Out the New
lesson.summary: Proactive interference occurs when information learned earlier makes it harder to learn or recall newer information, such as when years of typing an old password make a newly changed one stubbornly hard to remember.
lesson.body:
Proactive interference happens when something you learned in the past reaches forward in time and makes it harder to learn or recall something new. The word proactive here is being used in its literal sense of acting forward, not in the everyday sense of being prepared or taking initiative. Old material gets in the way of new material, rather than the reverse.

A familiar everyday example is changing a password or a phone number. For weeks after the change, people often catch themselves typing the old password out of habit, or find the new number strangely hard to keep straight in their head, even though they clearly understand and have consciously learned the new information. The old memory is not gone, and it is not simply that the new memory has not had time to solidify; the old, well practiced memory is actively competing with the new one every time you try to retrieve it, and often wins that competition by default because it is more deeply entrenched.

This connects directly back to the forgetting curve and complicates the simple picture of forgetting as pure decay over time. Researchers studying list learning found that when people learn several different lists of similar material in sequence, recall of the most recently learned list tends to get worse as the number of previously learned lists piles up, even when the amount of time since learning that last list is held constant. That pattern cannot be explained by decay alone, since the delay is the same each time. It points instead to interference: the more prior material competing for the same retrieval pathways, the harder it becomes to pull out the most recent addition. This build up pattern has been demonstrated across many repeated list learning experiments and is regarded as one of the more reliable findings in the memory literature, precisely because it is so easy to reproduce under controlled conditions.

Proactive interference shows up well beyond simple memorized lists. Someone who grew up speaking one language and later learns a second one often finds the grammar and pronunciation patterns of their first language bleeding into their attempts at the new one, a kind of proactive interference operating on language rules rather than on isolated facts. A similar effect shows up in physical skills, such as a driver who learned to drive on one side of the road struggling with old habits when driving in a country that uses the other side.

Proactive interference is really just one half of a two directional story about how memories compete with each other. It describes old material reaching forward to disrupt new learning. The mirror image of that process, where new material reaches backward to disrupt memory for what came before, is called retroactive interference, and it is just as common in everyday forgetting.
